entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 10 Zec 10:1-12 . Prayer and Promise. Call to prayer to Jehovah, as contrasted with the idol-worship which had brought judgments on the princes and people. Blessings promised in answer to prayer: (1) rulers of themselves; (2) conquest of their enemies; (3) restoration and establishment of both Israel and Judah in their own land in lasting peace and piety. 1. Ask ... rain-- on which the abundance of "corn" promised by the Lord ( Zec 9:17 ) depends. Jehovah alone can give it, and will give it on being asked ( Jr 10:13 ; 14:22 ). rain in ... time of ... latter rain-- that is, the latter rain in its due time, namely, in spring, about February or March ( Job 29:23 ; Joe 2:23 ). The latter rain ripened the grain, as the former rain in October tended to fructify the seed. Including all temporal blessings; these again being types of spiritual ones. Though God has begun to bless us, we are not to relax our prayers. The former rain of conversion may have been given, but we must also ask for the latter rain of ripened sanctification. Though at Pentecost there was a former rain on the Jewish Church, a latter rain is still to be looked for, when the full harvest of the nation's conversion shall be gathered in to God. The spirit of prayer in the Church is an index at once of her piety, and of the spiritual blessings she may expect from God. When the Church is full of prayer, God pours out a full blessing. bright clouds-- rather, "lightnings," the precursors of rain [Maurer]. showers of rain-- literally, "rain of heavy rain." In Job 37:6 the same words occur in inverted order [Henderson]. grass-- a general term, including both corn for men and grass for cattle.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13141"/><div sID="gen24756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13141"/><hi type="bold">2. idols--</hi>literally, "the teraphim," the household gods, consulted in divination (see on <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>). Derived by Gesenius from an Arabic root, "comfort," indicating them as the givers of comfort. Or an Ethiopian root, "relics." Herein Zechariah shows that the Jews by their own idolatry had stayed the grace of God heretofore, which otherwise would have given them all those blessings, temporal and spiritual, which they are now (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zec 10:1</reference>) urged to "ask" for.<div eID="gen24756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diviners--</hi>who gave responses to consulters of the teraphim: opposed to Jehovah and His true prophets.<div eID="gen24757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen a lie--</hi>pretending to see what they saw not in giving responses.<div eID="gen24758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comfort in vain--</hi>literally, "give vapor for comfort"; that is, give comforting promises to consulters which are sure to come to naught (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.2">16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">21:34</reference>).<div eID="gen24759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore they went their way--</hi>that is, Israel and Judah were led away captive.<div eID="gen24760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a flock ... no shepherd--</hi>As sheep wander and are a prey to every injury when without a shepherd, so the Jews had been while they were without Jehovah, the true shepherd; for the false prophets whom they trusted were no shepherds (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>). So now they are scattered, while they know not Messiah their shepherd; typified in the state of the disciples, when they had forsaken Jesus and fled (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">Mt 26:56</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zec 13:7</reference>). <div eID="gen24761" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13142"/><div sID="gen24762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13142"/><hi type="bold">3. against the shepherds--</hi>the civil rulers of Israel and Judah who abetted idolatry.<div eID="gen24762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">punished--</hi>literally, "visited upon." The same word "visited," without the upon, is presently after used in a good sense to heighten the contrast.<div eID="gen24763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goats--</hi>he-goats. As "shepherds" described what they ought to have been, so "he-goats" describes what they were, the emblem of headstrong wantonness and offensive lust (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Eze 34:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.5">Da 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">Mt 25:33</reference>). The he-goats head the flock. They who are first in crime will be first in punishment.<div eID="gen24764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visited--</hi>in mercy (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.68">Lu 1:68</reference>).<div eID="gen24765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as his goodly horse--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Zech.9.13">Zec 9:13</reference> they were represented under the image of bows and arrows, here under that of their commander-in-chief, Jehovah's battle horse (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>). God can make His people, timid though they be as sheep, courageous as the charger. The general rode on the most beautiful and richly caparisoned, and had his horse tended with the greatest care. Jehovah might cast off the Jews for their vileness, but He regards His election or adoption of them: whence He calls them here "His flock," and therefore saves them. <div eID="gen24766" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13143"/><div sID="gen24767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13143"/><hi type="bold">4. Out of him--</hi>Judah is to be no more subject to foreigners, but from itself shall come its rulers.<div eID="gen24767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the corner--</hi>stone, Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>). "Corners" simply express governors (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">1Sa 14:38</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Is 19:13</reference>, Margin). The Maccabees, Judah's governors and deliverers from Antiochus the oppressor, are primarily meant; but Messiah is the Antitype. Messiah supports and binds together the Church, Jews and Gentiles.<div eID="gen24768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the nail--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.4.21">Jud 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Is 22:23</reference>). The large peg inside an Oriental tent, on which is hung most of its valuable furniture. On Messiah hang all the glory and hope of His people.<div eID="gen24769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.9.13">Zec 9:13</reference>). Judah shall not need foreign soldiery. Messiah shall be her battle-bow (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">Psa 45:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Re 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen24770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every oppressor--</hi>rather, in a good sense, ruler, as the kindred Ethiopic term means. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13144"/><div sID="gen24772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13144"/><hi type="bold">5. riders on horses--</hi>namely, the enemy's horsemen. Though the Jews were forbidden by the law to multiply horses in battle (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>), they are made Jehovah's war horse (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>), and so tread down on foot the foe with all his cavalry (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.4">Eze 38:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.40">Da 11:40</reference>). Cavalry was the chief strength of the Syro-Grecian army (1 Maccabees 3:39). <div eID="gen24772" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13145"/><div sID="gen24773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13145"/><hi type="bold">6. Judah ... Joseph--</hi>that is, the ten tribes. The distinct mention of both Judah and Israel shows that there is yet a more complete restoration than that from Babylon, when Judah alone and a few Israelites from the other tribes returned. The Maccabean deliverance is here connected with it, just as the painter groups on the same canvas objects in the foreground and hills far distant; or as the comparatively near planet and the remote fixed star are seen together in the same firmament. Prophecy ever hastens to the glorious final consummation under Messiah.<div eID="gen24773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring them again to place them--</hi>namely, securely in their own land. The Hebrew verb is compounded of two, "I will bring again," and "I will place them" (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jr 32:37</reference>). Maurer, from a different form, translates, "I will make them to dwell." <div eID="gen24774" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13148"/><div sID="gen24782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13148"/><hi type="bold">9. sow them among ... people--</hi>Their dispersion was with a special design. Like seed sown far and wide, they shall, when quickened themselves, be the fittest instruments for quickening others (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). The slight hold they have on every soil where they now live, as also the commercial and therefore cosmopolitan character of their pursuits, making a change of residence easy to them, fit them peculiarly for missionary work [Moore]. The wide dispersion of the Jews just before Christ's coming prepared the way similarly for the apostles' preaching in the various Jewish synagogues throughout the world; everywhere some of the Old Testament seed previously sown was ready to germinate when the New Testament light and heat were brought to bear on it by Gospel preachers. Thus the way was opened for entrance among the Gentiles. "Will sow" is the Hebrew future, said of that which has been done, is being done, and may be done afterwards [Maurer], (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Ho 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen24782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall remember me in far countries--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1">De 30:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.37">2Ch 6:37</reference>). Implying the Jews' return to a right mind in "all the nations" where they are scattered simultaneously. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13150"/><div sID="gen24788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13150"/><hi type="bold">11. pass ... sea with affliction--</hi>Personifying the "sea"; He shall afflict the sea, that is, cause it to cease to be an obstacle to Israel's return to Palestine (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Is 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">16</reference>). Vulgate translates, "The strait of the sea." Maurer, "He shall cleave and smite." English Version is best (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">Psa 114:3</reference>). As Jehovah smote the Red Sea to make a passage for His people (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.16">Ex 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.21">21</reference>), so hereafter shall He make a way through every obstacle which opposes Israel's restoration.<div eID="gen24788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the river--</hi>the Nile (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Am 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">9:5</reference>), or the Euphrates. Thus the Red Sea and the Euphrates in the former part of the verse answer to "Assyria" and "Egypt" in the latter.<div eID="gen24789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sceptre of Egypt ... depart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference>). <div eID="gen24790" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.title: Zec 10:1-12 . Prayer and Promise.
navigation_sections.content_plain: Zec 10:1-12 . Prayer and Promise. Call to prayer to Jehovah, as contrasted with the idol-worship which had brought judgments on the princes and people. Blessings promised in answer to prayer: (1) rulers of themselves; (2) conquest of their enemies; (3) restoration and establishment of both Israel and Judah in their own land in lasting peace and piety.
